subtitulo: Saying something difficult so that it can be acted on
descripcion: Feedback in English professional culture follows conventions strong enough to learn as formulas. The core one: describe behaviour and impact, not character. *You were unprepared* is character; *the deck arrived an hour before the meeting, so we spent fifteen minutes reading* is behaviour and impact — and only the second gives the person something to change.

ejemplos.texto: *Can I give you some feedback on the report? Two things worked, one didn't.*
*When the estimate changed without a note, the client assumed we'd hidden it. That's the bit I'd do differently.*
*I might be missing context — what's your read on why it slipped?*
*What's your read on why it slipped?*

notas: Asking permission first is near-mandatory in most English-speaking workplaces.
The praise-criticism-praise sandwich is now widely disliked: people hear only the praise, or wait for the middle.
Naming your own uncertainty makes the feedback easier to accept without weakening it.
errores: *You always* / *You never* — indefensible, and guarantees defensiveness.
Softening until the message is invisible. If they leave unsure there was a problem, there wasn't one.
Feedback on personality rather than output.

When X happened, the effect was Y

traducciones.es: eso es lo que yo haría distinto

redemittel.expresion: How do you want to handle it?

mision.consigna: Give written feedback to a colleague on something that genuinely went wrong.
requisitos: one acknowledged limit of your own view

microtareas.texto: Rewrite three character judgements (*careless*, *disorganised*, *defensive*) as behaviour plus impact.
Write one piece of feedback in three sentences. Cut it to two.
Record 90 seconds of feedback aloud. Listen back: did you soften it into invisibility?

autochequeo: Is every point behaviour, or did a character judgement slip in?
Is the impact stated, or only implied?
Would the person leave knowing exactly what to change?
Did I ask permission and hand the turn back?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the feedback. (1) Mark each point as behaviour or character. (2) Is the impact stated or only implied? (3) Would the person know exactly what to change? (4) Flag where I softened it into invisibility. Do not rewrite the text.

filas: Can I give you some feedback on the report?
When the estimate changed without a note…
What's your read on why it slipped?
I might be missing context here.

contraste.es: Spanish workplace feedback tends to be either indirect to the point of invisibility or blunt and personal. English has a well-defined middle register for which Spanish lacks a fixed formula — which is why learning the four slots is worth more here than learning vocabulary.
